text: Every command from this chapter is useful typed by hand once, but real administration means running the same checks over and over, on multiple servers, without retyping them every time. A shell script is just those commands saved into a file so they run together, automatically — the direct foundation for the automation tools later in this course.

Every bash script starts with a shebang, hash-bang-slash-bin-slash-bash, telling the system which program should run the rest of the file. A variable stores a value under a name you choose — SERVICE equals nginx, no spaces around the equals sign — and reading it back requires a dollar sign in front, dollar-SERVICE, to tell bash to substitute the stored value.

An if statement runs a block only when a condition is true, closed with fi. systemctl is-active --quiet exits successfully if a service is running, which is exactly the kind of check if reacts to. A for loop repeats a block once per item in a list, closed with done — looping over syslog and auth.log to tail each one in turn.

Put together — shebang, a variable, an if block checking whether nginx is running, a for loop tailing both log files — that's a complete, real script. Save it as check-services dot sh. One more step is required before it will run: chmod +x marks the file executable, and then dot-slash runs it from the current directory.

This exact pattern is the building block every cloud automation tool in this program relies on: a startup script that runs the moment a cloud VM boots, a health check called on a schedule, a deployment step run across a dozen servers at once. Everything ahead on virtualization and the cloud assumes you're comfortable writing exactly this.

That closes out Chapter 4, Linux Fundamentals II. Chapter 5 moves into Virtualization Fundamentals, starting with what virtualization actually is — the real difference between a Type 1 and a Type 2 hypervisor, and why the cloud couldn't exist without either one.
